learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected First-price and locked the rule predicted to earn most with two random-value bidders bidding optimally.
observations.exploration: Ran one auction, then all 20,000. Average higher and lower values were $66.6 and $33.4. Inspected second-price, first-price and all-pay modes: average seller revenues were $33.4, $33.3 and $33.3. The last values were A $90.0 and B $18.9: second-price charged A $18.9, first-price A $45.0, and all-pay A $40.5 plus B $1.8.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to about the same, accurately quoted my 20,000 averages and last-auction contrast, and explained strategic bid changes offset payment rules. It connected second-price to lower value, first-price to half the higher value, and all-pay to smaller bids from both. It disclosed independent uniform values and optimal bidding.
observations.visual: Inspected inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshots in all three payment modes. Three almost equal revenue bars met a dashed theory line at $33.3; the selected bar was filled. A lower value line and payment bars showed different last-auction payments under the same underlying values.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The prompt challenges comparing payment rules while holding bids mentally fixed.
prediction.evidence: Selected first-price before optimal bid adaptation was visible.

interaction.reason: Large-sample averages and per-auction rule modes separate two levels of comparison.
interaction.evidence: Average revenues matched closely while the same last auction charged $18.9 versus $45.0.

payoff.reason: The reveal uses actual means to explain why bid adaptation cancels the payment difference.
payoff.evidence: Half of the higher-value mean 66.6 matches the lower-value mean 33.4 approximately.

clarity.reason: Separate aggregate bars and last-auction payments prevent conflating one sale with expectation.
clarity.evidence: Theory and sampled means are labelled separately.

transfer.reason: The strategic principle is explained but no new auction assumptions or application are developed.
transfer.evidence: All tested cases retain two independent uniform-value optimal bidders.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Making the winner pay their own bid need not raise average seller revenue.
surprise.evidence: All three sample means were about $33.3.

visualExplanation.reason: The display juxtaposes equal means with different individual payments.
visualExplanation.evidence: The three top bars nearly match while the lower payment bars vary by rule.

playfulness.reason: Sampling and payment mode switches provide controlled investigation.
playfulness.evidence: The learner can inspect the same values under three rules.

practicalValue.reason: It illustrates why changing a rule can change participant behavior.
practicalValue.evidence: The reveal states that bid responses offset the direct payment change.

depth.reason: The lesson includes sample variation, individual outcomes and model assumptions.
depth.evidence: A single auction differs while theoretical averages match under explicit conditions.

complexity.reason: The controls are easy, but strategic bidding and expected order statistics require several unfamiliar concepts.
complexity.conceptualDemand: High: separate valuations, bids, payments and average revenue across rules.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low to moderate: sample buttons and three modes control a two-level display.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: A rule's direct payment effect is offset by equilibrium behavior.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: First-price, second-price, all-pay and optimal bid shading are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Moderate: aggregate bars, theory line, valuation positions and individual payment bars.

whyCool: Three very different ways of charging bidders converge to the same average because the bidders adapt.
caveat: The equivalence is shown under fixed ideal assumptions, not as a universal claim about actual auctions.
missingEvidence: No alternative value distribution, bidder count or nonoptimal strategy was tested.
